title: Which numbers should you know by heart for market sizing?
description: Rough population, household and time figures that make market sizing faster, plus how to use them and what to do when you do not know a number.
hook: Market sizing is much less stressful when you have a few anchor numbers in your head. You do not need to memorise statistics; interviewers care about your logic, and they will often give you a number if you ask. But knowing a handful of round figures lets you start confidently. Here are the ones worth having, rounded the way you would use them in a case.
body:
People (rounded, recent estimates)

  • World: about 8 billion
  • India and China: about 1.4 billion each
  • United States: about 340 million (342 million in 2025)
  • European Union: about 450 million
  • United Kingdom: about 69 million (69.3 million at mid-2024)
  • Germany: about 84 million; France: about 68 million
  • London: about 9 million; New York City: about 8 million

Households

  • Average household size: about 2.4 people in the UK, about 2.5 in the US
  • So the UK has roughly 28.6 million households (2024), and the US roughly 129 million

Time

  • Days in a year: 365; weeks: 52; hours: about 8,760
  • Working days in a year: about 220 to 250, depending on holidays
  • Working hours in a year for one full-time person: about 1,800 to 2,000
  • Life expectancy in rich countries: about 80 years, a handy way to turn a population into "people of each age" (population ÷ 80 is a rough number per year of age)

When you do not know a number

Say so, and make a sensible assumption out loud: "I don't know the exact number of UK households, so I'll assume about 28 million, from 68 million people and around 2.4 per home." Or ask: "Do we have a figure for that?" Both are fine. What is not fine is freezing, or inventing a precise number without explaining it.

Round, and say you are rounding

Use numbers that make the maths easy: 68 million becomes 70 million, 52 weeks becomes 50. Say "I'll round to 70 million to keep the maths simple." Then, at the end, check whether the rounding pushed the answer meaningfully up or down.

Figures change over time, so treat these as rough anchors for practice, not facts to quote.

Use anchor numbers carefully

A few rounded benchmarks can speed up market sizing, but a memorised population is not the answer. Consider the difference between estimating the number of households and the number of people. For an illustrative country with 60 million people and 2.5 people per household, there are about 24 million households. If you accidentally use the population where the formula requires households, your answer may be inflated by a factor of 2.5.

Always label assumptions by year, geography and definition. A population estimate from 2024 may be acceptable as a round interview anchor in 2026, but should not be presented as an exact current statistic. Likewise, the number of working adults is not the number of households, and a company's market share by revenue is not necessarily its share by units.

The fastest way to build fluency is to remember rough orders of magnitude and derive smaller numbers. If you know the population and plausible household size, you can estimate homes; if you know births per year and lifespan, you can cross-check age cohorts. When a result looks surprising, re-check the unit before changing the assumption.
